questions.stem: Balance day adjustments are made at the end of a reporting period mainly to apply which accounting assumption?
options: the accounting entity assumption
the historical cost assumption
the accrual basis assumption
the going concern assumption
questions.explanation: Balance day adjustments make sure revenue is recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, even if the cash moves in another period, which is the accrual basis. The entity assumption is about separating the owner's affairs, not about timing.

questions.stem: Why must Magpie Music Supplies record balance day adjustments before preparing its Income Statement for the year ended 30 June?
options: so that the Trial Balance totals agree before the General Ledger is balanced
so that the GST owed to the Australian Taxation Office can be calculated
so that the report includes only the revenue earned and expenses incurred in that year
so that the report includes every cash receipt and payment made during that year
questions.explanation: The period and accrual basis assumptions require profit to be measured from the revenue and expenses that belong to the year, which cash records alone do not show. A report of every cash receipt and payment is the Cash Flow Statement.

questions.stem: Under the asset approach, a payment in advance for twelve months' insurance is first recorded by debiting:
options: Insurance Expense, an expense
Accrued Insurance, a current liability
Unearned Insurance, a current liability
Prepaid Insurance, a current asset
questions.explanation: The asset approach records the whole prepayment as an asset, because the business has paid for future benefits, and transfers the used part to expense at balance day. Debiting the expense first would be the expense approach, which the study design does not use.

questions.stem: On 1 April Magpie Music Supplies paid $2,640 including GST for twelve months' insurance. Which entry records the payment?
options: Dr Prepaid Insurance 2,400; Dr GST Clearing 240; Cr Bank 2,640
Dr Prepaid Insurance 2,640; Cr Bank 2,640
Dr Insurance Expense 2,400; Dr GST Clearing 240; Cr Bank 2,640
Dr Prepaid Insurance 2,400; Cr GST Clearing 240; Cr Bank 2,160
questions.explanation: For a prepaid expense the study design records GST at the time of payment, so $240 goes to GST Clearing and the $2,400 prepayment is an asset. Recording the full $2,640 as the asset would leave the GST unclaimed.

questions.stem: The insurance prepaid on 1 April ($2,400 excluding GST for twelve months) is adjusted at 30 June. Which balance day adjustment is recorded?
options: Dr Insurance Expense 1,800; Cr Prepaid Insurance 1,800
Dr Prepaid Insurance 600; Cr Insurance Expense 600
Dr Insurance Expense 660; Cr Prepaid Insurance 660
Dr Insurance Expense 600; Cr Prepaid Insurance 600
questions.explanation: Three months of cover (April to June) has been used, so 3/12 × $2,400 = $600 moves from the asset to the expense, leaving $1,800 prepaid. GST was dealt with at payment, so it is not part of the adjustment.

questions.stem: Magpie Music Supplies paid $13,200 including GST on 1 March for twelve months' rent. What is reported for rent at the year end of 30 June?
options: Rent Expense $4,400; Prepaid Rent $8,800
Rent Expense $12,000; Prepaid Rent nil
Rent Expense $4,000; Prepaid Rent $8,000
Rent Expense $8,000; Prepaid Rent $4,000
questions.explanation: Excluding GST the rent is $12,000, or $1,000 a month; March to June is four months, so $4,000 is expense and $8,000 remains a current asset. Including GST in the split gives $4,400 and $8,800, but the GST was recorded separately at payment.

questions.stem: If Magpie Music Supplies forgets the balance day adjustment for insurance used, what is the effect on its reports?
options: Expenses overstated, net profit understated, current assets understated
Expenses understated, net profit overstated, current liabilities understated
No effect on profit, but cash in the Balance Sheet is overstated
Expenses understated, net profit overstated, current assets overstated
questions.explanation: Without the adjustment the used insurance stays in Prepaid Insurance, so the asset is too high and the expense too low, overstating profit. Cash is unaffected because the payment was recorded correctly when it was made.

questions.stem: An accrued expense is:
options: an expense paid in the period for a future period
an expense paid and used up in the same period
an expense that will be incurred in the next period
an expense incurred in the period but not yet paid
questions.explanation: An accrued expense has been incurred, so it belongs in this period's profit, but the payment has not yet been made, creating a liability. An expense paid in advance for a future period is a prepaid expense.

questions.stem: At 30 June Magpie Music Supplies owes its staff $3,000 in wages for the last few days of June, to be paid on 4 July. Which balance day adjustment is recorded?
options: Dr Accrued Wages 3,000; Cr Wages 3,000
Dr Wages 3,000; Cr Bank 3,000
Dr Prepaid Wages 3,000; Cr Wages 3,000
Dr Wages 3,000; Cr Accrued Wages 3,000
questions.explanation: The wages were incurred in June, so the expense is recognised now with a current liability for the amount owing. Bank is not credited because nothing is paid until July.

questions.stem: On 4 July Magpie Music Supplies pays wages of $5,000, which include the $3,000 accrued at 30 June. Which entry records the payment?
options: Dr Accrued Wages 3,000; Dr Wages 2,000; Cr Bank 5,000
Dr Wages 5,000; Cr Bank 5,000
Dr Accrued Wages 5,000; Cr Bank 5,000
Dr Accrued Wages 3,000; Dr Wages 5,000; Cr Bank 8,000
questions.explanation: The $3,000 for June settles the liability recorded at balance day, and only the $2,000 for July is this period's expense. Debiting Wages with the whole $5,000 would count June's $3,000 as an expense in two different periods.

questions.stem: At 30 June an electricity account of $300 (excluding GST) was accrued. On 20 July the business paid $440 including GST, covering June's $300 and $100 for July. Which entry records the payment?
options: Dr Electricity 400; Dr GST Clearing 40; Cr Bank 440
Dr Accrued Electricity 400; Dr GST Clearing 40; Cr Bank 440
Dr Accrued Electricity 300; Dr Electricity 100; Dr GST Clearing 40; Cr Bank 440
Dr Accrued Electricity 330; Dr Electricity 110; Cr Bank 440
questions.explanation: The study design records GST on an accrued expense at the time of payment, so the whole $40 of GST on the $400 bill is claimed now, the $300 liability is settled and $100 is July's expense. Charging all $400 to Electricity would expense June's portion a second time.

questions.stem: Under the study design, when is GST recorded for an accrued expense?
options: when the accrued expense is paid in the subsequent period
in the balance day adjustment at the end of the period
half at balance day and half when the account is paid
never, because accrued expenses do not attract GST
questions.explanation: No cash or tax invoice has been dealt with at balance day, so the adjustment records the expense and liability excluding GST, and the GST is recorded when the account is paid. Many accrued expenses, such as electricity, do attract GST.

questions.stem: Interest of $500 on the business loan has been incurred for June but will not be paid until July. How does recording this accrual affect the working capital ratio at 30 June?
options: It decreases the ratio, because current assets decrease.
It increases the ratio, because current liabilities decrease.
It decreases the ratio, because current liabilities increase.
It increases the ratio, because current assets increase.
questions.explanation: Accrued Interest is a current liability, so recording it raises current liabilities with no change to current assets, lowering the working capital ratio. No cash is paid at balance day, so current assets are unchanged.

questions.stem: During the year Magpie Music Supplies paid wages of $80,000. Accrued wages were $2,000 at the start of the year and $3,000 at the end. What is Wages expense for the year?
questions.explanation: The $2,000 paid for last year's accrual is not this year's expense, and the $3,000 still owing at year end is, so $80,000 − $2,000 + $3,000 = $81,000. Reversing the adjustments gives $79,000, and using the cash paid alone ignores the accrual basis.

questions.stem: Under the liability approach, a deposit received from a customer for goods to be supplied next month is recorded as:
options: Capital, an increase in owner's equity
Unearned Revenue, a current liability
Sales, a revenue
Accrued Revenue, a current asset
questions.explanation: The business has received cash but still owes the customer the goods, so the deposit is a liability until it is earned. Recording it as Sales would recognise revenue before the goods are supplied.

questions.stem: In VCE Accounting, no GST is recorded when a deposit is received for goods not yet supplied. On 25 June Magpie Music Supplies receives a $2,000 deposit on a piano to be delivered in August. Which entry is recorded?
options: Dr Bank 2,000; Cr Unearned Revenue 1,818; Cr GST Clearing 182
Dr Bank 2,000; Cr Sales 2,000
Dr Unearned Revenue 2,000; Cr Bank 2,000
Dr Bank 2,000; Cr Unearned Revenue 2,000
questions.explanation: The study design records unearned revenue using the liability approach, with no GST recorded at the time of the deposit, so the full $2,000 is credited to Unearned Revenue. Splitting out $182 of GST may reflect some real tax situations, but the study design specifically excludes GST at this point.

questions.stem: Where does the $2,000 piano deposit appear in the reports for the year ended 30 June?
options: revenue in the Income Statement and an operating inflow in the Cash Flow Statement
a current liability in the Balance Sheet only, because it is not yet earned
a financing inflow in the Cash Flow Statement and a current liability in the Balance Sheet
an operating inflow in the Cash Flow Statement and a current liability in the Balance Sheet
questions.explanation: The cash has been received from a customer in June, so it is an operating inflow now, while the obligation to deliver the piano makes it a current liability. It is not revenue until the piano is delivered.

questions.stem: Magpie Music Supplies holds $6,000 of Unearned Revenue for lessons paid in advance. At 30 June, $2,500 of the lessons have been given. Ignoring GST, what is the effect of the balance day adjustment?
options: Liabilities −$2,500 and net profit +$2,500, with no change to cash
Liabilities −$2,500 and cash +$2,500, with no change to profit
Liabilities +$2,500 and net profit −$2,500, with no change to cash
Liabilities −$3,500 and net profit +$3,500, with no change to cash
questions.explanation: The lessons given have been earned, so $2,500 moves from the Unearned Revenue liability to revenue, increasing profit. The cash arrived when the deposit was paid, so the adjustment involves no cash.

questions.stem: If a business records a customer's deposit for next year's goods directly as Sales, what is the effect on this year's reports?
options: Net profit overstated and current assets overstated
Net profit correct but cash overstated
Net profit overstated and current liabilities understated
Net profit understated and current liabilities overstated
questions.explanation: Revenue that has not yet been earned is reported this year, overstating profit, and the obligation to supply the goods is left out of liabilities. Cash is correct because the deposit was genuinely received.

questions.stem: Accrued revenue is reported in the Balance Sheet as:
options: a current asset
a current liability
a non-current asset
part of owner's equity
questions.explanation: Accrued revenue has been earned but not yet received, so the business has a right to receive it within the coming year, a current asset. Unearned revenue is the liability, where cash has been received before it is earned.

questions.stem: At 30 June Magpie Music Supplies has earned $800 commission on instrument hire arranged for a manufacturer, but has not yet received it. Which balance day adjustment is recorded?
options: Dr Commission Revenue 800; Cr Accrued Commission Revenue 800
Dr Bank 800; Cr Commission Revenue 800
Dr Accrued Commission Revenue 800; Cr Commission Revenue 800
Dr Accrued Commission Revenue 880; Cr Commission Revenue 800; Cr GST Clearing 80
questions.explanation: The commission has been earned in June, so revenue is recognised with a current asset for the amount receivable. The study design records GST on accrued revenue at the time of receipt, so no GST is recorded at balance day.

questions.stem: On 15 July the business receives $1,320 including GST, covering the $800 commission accrued at 30 June and $400 earned in July. Which entry records the receipt?
options: Dr Bank 1,320; Cr Accrued Commission Revenue 1,200; Cr GST Clearing 120
Dr Bank 1,320; Cr Accrued Commission Revenue 800; Cr Commission Revenue 400; Cr GST Clearing 120
Dr Bank 1,320; Cr Commission Revenue 1,200; Cr GST Clearing 120
Dr Bank 1,320; Cr Accrued Commission Revenue 880; Cr Commission Revenue 440
questions.explanation: The receipt settles the $800 asset, recognises only July's $400 as revenue and records the GST of $120 on the full $1,200, because GST on accrued revenue is recorded when it is received. Crediting all $1,200 to revenue would count June's $800 in two periods.

questions.stem: If a business fails to record accrued interest revenue of $600 on its term deposit at balance day, what is the effect?
options: Net profit and current liabilities are both overstated by $600.
Net profit is understated and cash is understated by $600.
Net profit is overstated and current assets are understated by $600.
Net profit and current assets are both understated by $600.
questions.explanation: The interest was earned this period, so leaving it out understates revenue, profit and the asset of accrued revenue. No cash was due to be received at balance day, so cash is correct.

questions.stem: During the year a business received rent revenue of $14,000 in cash. Accrued rent revenue was $1,000 at the start of the year and $1,500 at the end. What is Rent Revenue for the year (ignore GST)?
questions.explanation: Of the cash received, $1,000 belonged to last year, and $1,500 earned this year has not yet been received: $14,000 − $1,000 + $1,500 = $14,500. Reversing the two adjustments gives $13,500.

questions.stem: An adjusted Trial Balance is prepared:
options: before balance day adjustments, to find which adjustments are needed
after closing entries, to check that revenue and expenses are now zero
at the start of the next period, to record opening balances
after balance day adjustments, to check the ledger before reports are prepared
questions.explanation: The adjusted Trial Balance lists the General Ledger balances once balance day adjustments are posted, checking that debits equal credits and giving the figures used for the reports. It comes before the closing entries, which reduce revenue and expense accounts to zero.

questions.stem: Which account appears in the adjusted Trial Balance but would NOT appear in the post-closing ledger at the start of the next period?
options: Insurance Expense
Prepaid Insurance
Accrued Wages
Unearned Revenue
questions.explanation: Insurance Expense is closed to the Profit and Loss Summary at the end of the period, so it starts the next period at zero. Prepaid Insurance, Accrued Wages and Unearned Revenue are assets and liabilities, so their balances are carried forward.

questions.stem: A business's unadjusted Trial Balance totals $420,000 on each side. It then records accrued wages of $3,000 and transfers $2,000 of prepaid rent to expense. What are the adjusted Trial Balance totals?
options: $421,000 on each side
$423,000 on each side
$425,000 on each side
$420,000 on each side
questions.explanation: Accrued wages add a new $3,000 debit to Wages and a new $3,000 credit balance in Accrued Wages, so both totals rise by $3,000. The prepaid rent transfer just moves $2,000 of debit from one asset to an expense, leaving the totals unchanged, so they are $423,000.

questions.stem: Which statement about balance day adjustments is correct?
options: They affect only the Balance Sheet, because they record assets and liabilities.
They affect the Income Statement and Balance Sheet but not the Cash Flow Statement.
They affect the Cash Flow Statement and Balance Sheet but not the Income Statement.
They affect all three reports, because each one involves a cash movement.
questions.explanation: Each adjustment changes a revenue or expense and an asset or liability, but none involves cash on balance day, so the Cash Flow Statement is unaffected. The cash for a prepayment or deposit moved when it was paid or received, not at the adjustment.

questions.stem: How is the Prepaid Rent of $8,000 treated when calculating the quick assets ratio?
options: It is added to current liabilities, because it is rent owing.
It is deducted from inventory before the ratio is calculated.
It is excluded from quick assets, along with inventory.
It is included in quick assets, because it is a current asset.
questions.explanation: The quick assets ratio deducts inventory and prepayments from current assets, because neither can be turned quickly into cash to pay debts. Prepaid rent is an asset, not an amount owing.

questions.stem: Magpie Music Supplies made a net profit of $40,000, but its net cash flow from operating activities was $46,000. Which balance day item could help explain this?
options: Accrued expenses fell: more of last year's expenses were paid this year.
Unearned revenue rose: customers paid deposits for goods not yet supplied.
Prepaid expenses rose: more expenses were paid in advance for next year.
Accrued revenue rose: more revenue was earned but not yet received.
questions.explanation: Deposits received for goods not yet supplied bring in cash before any revenue is recognised, so cash exceeds profit. Higher prepayments, higher accrued revenue and paying off accruals all leave cash below profit.

questions.stem: Which item recorded at balance day reduces net profit for the period without any change in cash in that period?
options: a deposit received from a customer for goods to be delivered next period
accrued revenue for commission earned but not yet received
the payment of twelve months' insurance in advance under the asset approach
an accrued expense for electricity used but not yet billed
questions.explanation: An accrued expense increases expenses now, reducing profit, while the cash is paid next period. Accrued revenue increases profit, a customer's deposit does not affect profit when received, and paying insurance in advance involves cash.

questions.stem: Which balance day adjustment increases current assets?
options: recording accrued revenue
recording an accrued expense
transferring prepaid rent used to expense
recording unearned revenue now earned
questions.explanation: Accrued revenue creates a receivable, a current asset. Transferring used prepaid rent to expense reduces a current asset, while an accrued expense and the earning of unearned revenue affect liabilities.

questions.stem: The electricity bill for April to June arrives on 10 July. The accountant uses it to record an accrued expense in the June reports. Which qualitative characteristics does this support?
options: faithful representation and verifiability, because the amount is based on a document
timeliness and comparability, because the bill arrived after the period ended
understandability only, because owners find accrued expenses easier to read
relevance only, because the bill relates to the next reporting period
questions.explanation: Using the actual bill makes the accrued expense complete and accurate, and the bill is a source document that allows the amount to be checked. The bill relates to the June quarter, not the next period.

questions.stem: The owner of Magpie Music Supplies asks the accountant not to record $9,000 of accrued wages at 30 June because a buyer for the business is reviewing the reports. What is the main ethical problem?
options: The GST owed would be understated, so the business would pay too little tax.
Profit and the business's position would be overstated, misleading the buyer.
Profit would be understated, so the owner would receive too little for the business.
The cash balance would be overstated, so the buyer would pay too much.
questions.explanation: Leaving out the accrual understates expenses and liabilities by $9,000, so profit and net assets look better than they are, deliberately misleading a user of the reports. Cash is unaffected because the wages have not been paid.

questions.stem: On 1 May a business paid $3,300 including GST for an advertising campaign to run in May, June and July. What is Advertising Expense at the 30 June year end?
questions.explanation: Excluding GST the campaign costs $3,000, or $1,000 a month, and May and June are two months, so $2,000 is expensed and $1,000 remains prepaid. Including GST in the split gives $2,200.

questions.stem: During the year a business paid $5,000 (excluding GST) for insurance. Prepaid insurance was $1,200 at the start of the year and $1,500 at the end. What is Insurance Expense for the year?
questions.explanation: Last year's prepayment of $1,200 is used up this year, and $1,500 of this year's payments is for next year: $1,200 + $5,000 − $1,500 = $4,700. Reversing the two adjustments gives $5,300.

questions.stem: A prepaid expense is reported in the Balance Sheet as:
options: a current liability
an expense
part of owner's equity
a current asset
questions.explanation: A prepaid expense is a payment for benefits the business has yet to receive, so it is a current asset until it is used up. It becomes an expense only as the benefit is consumed.

questions.stem: Accrued wages owing to staff at balance day are reported as:
options: a reduction in cash
a current liability
a current asset
a non-current liability
questions.explanation: The business owes the wages and will pay them within weeks, so they are a current liability. No cash has been paid yet, so Bank is unaffected at balance day.
